2611.03032v1.authors: Xiaofei Wu, Rongmei Liang, Jian Qing Shi
2611.03032v1.ori_summary: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.

2611.03026v1.title: Improved regret bounds in tabular RL under local differential privacy
2611.03026v1.ori_summary: We study regret minimization for time-homogeneous episodic tabular reinforcement learning with $S$ states and $A$ actions under non-interactive $ε$-local differential privacy (LDP). In each episode $k \in [K]$, the decision-maker sends a policy to a user, the user executes the policy for $H$ steps, and sends an $ε$-locally differentially private message back to the decision-maker. When $H=1$, the problem reduces to an LDP contextual bandit with $S$ contexts, $A$ arms and horizon $K$. We prove that the minimax regret is $\min\bigg(K, \frac{ \sqrt{\max( S, \exp(ε) + 1) S A K (\exp(ε) + 1)}}{\exp(ε) - 1}\bigg)$, up to constants and a $\sqrt{\log(A)}$ factor. The upper bound is achieved by an adaptation of EXP3 and a unary encoding mechanism. When $H > 1$, and for small $ε$, we show a lower bound in $Ω(HS\frac{\sqrt{A K}}ε)$ and an upper bound in $\tilde{O}(H^2 S^2 \frac{\sqrt{ AK}}ε)$. The upper bound is achieved by an algorithm based on UCBVI and a unary encoding mechanism. For small $ε$, these bounds improve the previously known lower bound by a factor $\sqrt{S}$ and the previously known upper bound by a factor of $H \sqrt{A}$.

2611.03020v1.title: The Tower of Babel in artificial intelligence: who should speak, and when it pays to listen
2611.03020v1.ori_summary: Two machines can each recognize an object well and still fail together. We study classifiers that see different parts of one object and send short messages to a receiver that identifies its class. Coordination asks how to design messages together; cooperation asks whether the team outperforms one sender given the whole budget. On three digit datasets, messages designed together beat messages designed apart by 18.07 to 22.68 percentage points on average with two-bit messages, with gains in all 24 configurations. A fixed agreement, you report the row and I the column, recovers about half this gain, with only the receiver learned. Senders that draw the same distinctions waste a narrow vocabulary, and senders whose distinctions cross multiply it. A team has no more possible messages than one sender with the same budget, so a partner must bring evidence the first lacks. A solvable model shows individual statistics alone cannot determine whether a partnership helps. On MNIST digits, six shared bits remove 49.54 percent of the strongest tested solo's errors on average. Paired measurements correctly predicted most sensor teams would reduce average accuracy on new participants. Who should speak is a property of the pair, and must be measured in pairs.

2611.02981v1.title: Utility-Aware Generative Recommendation: Utility-Enriched Semantic Codes and Utility-Guided Decoding
2611.02981v1.authors: Yang Hu, Duo Wang, Ning Li, Kang Li, Junda She, Chengcheng Guo, Kuo Cai, Bin Liu, Youhua Liu, Xiaoshuang Chen
2611.02981v1.ori_summary: Generative recommendation has been widely adopted in large-scale industrial recommendation systems, where multimodal item embeddings are quantized into offline semantic identifiers (SIDs) and items are retrieved by autoregressively generating their SIDs. However, conventional SID construction often underrepresents item utility reflected in post-exposure behaviors such as shares, long views, and video completion, making semantically similar items with different utility insufficiently distinguishable while struggling to accommodate rapidly changing utility signals. Moreover, generation likelihood may be misaligned with downstream utility, causing high-utility candidates to be prematurely pruned during beam search before post-generation reranking or training-time reward alignment can effectively compensate. To address these limitations, we propose UAGR, which aligns both SID construction and decoding with downstream multi-objective utility. Our Utility-Enriched Semantic Codes preserve the original semantic information while incorporating item-level utility without increasing SID length or vocabulary size, supporting incremental utility updates with no additional tokenization or sequence-decoding cost. Meanwhile, our Utility-Guided Decoding estimates candidate utility by combining predictions of multiple post-exposure outcomes and incorporates these estimates into beam scoring, reducing the risk of prematurely pruning high-utility paths while enabling flexible utility control without interfering with generative backbone training. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B tests under real-world traffic demonstrate the effectiveness and deployability of UAGR, which has been fully deployed on Kuaishou and increases video watch time by 0.206\% online.

2611.02966v1.title: SHq: Learnable Grids for LLM Weight Quantization
2611.02966v1.authors: Michael Helcig, Earl Killian, Dan Alistarh
2611.02966v1.ori_summary: Block-scaled lookup-table (LUT) formats, which represent weights as indices into a small value set (the grid), have become standard for low-bit LLM quantization, ranging from NF4 and BOF4 to the 3-bit LUT instruction in NVIDIA Rubin. While these formats leave the grid definition flexible, existing implementations rely on fixed grids derived either from numerical data types (INT, FP) or assumed weight distributions (NF, BOF). We demonstrate that no single fixed grid is universally optimal; the best fixed grid varies with bit-width: BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and INT at 6 bits. We introduce SHq, a closed-form family of grids parameterized by two critical degrees of freedom: a companding strength α that interpolates level spacing from uniform to floating-point-like, and an offset c that introduces asymmetry. This offset allows the sign bit of the FP8 block scale, otherwise unused, to select between the grid and its mirror image, up to doubling the number of distinct values available per block. SHq modifies only the lookup table contents and serves as a drop-in replacement for the grid in any such format. Across five models ranging from 3B to 35B parameters, including a mixture-of-experts architecture, evaluated at 2-6 bits using RTN and GPTQ, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in every setting at 3 and 4 bits and in most settings at 2, 5 and 6 bits. It outperforms the best fixed grid by up to 34% and remains superior under mixed-precision configurations. At 4.5 bits per weight, the SHq format reduces the KL divergence of NVFP4 by 41-67% while improving downstream accuracy. Grid families incorporating both spacing and offset parameters perform comparably, whereas those lacking an offset exhibit clearly higher error, confirming that these two degrees of freedom drive the observed gains. We therefore propose SHq as the standard grid for block-scaled lookup-table formats.

2611.02964v1.title: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time
2611.02964v1.authors: Sadman Rakib Pinon, Adamo Orsini, Yanis Falaki, Linlian Jiang, Jacob Kingi, Yang Wang, Xinxin Zuo
2611.02964v1.ori_summary: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.

2611.03548v1.title: Mediating Human-Swarm Interactions Through a Robot Helper: A Shepherding-Inspired Approach
2611.03548v1.authors: Arihant Yadav, Sophie Jörg, Eakta Jain
2611.03548v1.ori_summary: This work investigates human-swarm interaction (HSI) for steering large collectives through an intermediary robot helper. While prior robot-swarm control and HSI techniques commonly assume swarm members are addressable, these assumptions often fail for ``ungovernable'' swarms such as wildlife flocks and schools of fish. Motivated by pastoral shepherding, we compare low-level teleoperation to a higher-autonomy motion-primitives interface in a virtual reality (VR) shepherding task under varied swarm cohesion dynamics. Results indicate that motion primitives that operate on collective shape (e.g., boundary-based control) improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.

2611.03516v1.title: EmbryoProfiler: A Visual Clinical Decision Support System for IVF
2611.03516v1.authors: Johannes Knittel, Simon Warchol, Jakob Troidl, Camelia D. Brumar, Helen Yu Yang, Eric Mörth, Robert Krüger, Daniel Needleman, Dalit Ben-Yosef, Hanspeter Pfister
2611.03516v1.ori_summary: In-vitro fertilization (IVF) has become standard practice to address infertility, which affects more than one in ten couples in the US. However, current protocols yield relatively low success rates of about 20% per treatment cycle. A critical but complex and time-consuming step is the grading and selection of embryos for implantation. Although incubators with time-lapse microscopy have enabled computational analysis of embryo development, existing automated approaches either require extensive manual annotations or use opaque deep learning models that are hard for clinicians to validate and trust. We present EmbryoProfiler, a visual analytics system collaboratively developed with embryologists, biologists, and machine learning researchers to support clinicians in visually assessing embryo viability from time-lapse microscopy imagery. Our system incorporates a deep learning pipeline that automatically annotates microscopy images and extracts clinically interpretable features relevant for embryo grading. Our contributions include: (1) a semi-automatic, visualization-based workflow that guides clinicians through fertilization assessment, developmental timing evaluation, morphological inspection, and comparative analysis of embryos; (2) innovative interactive visualizations, such as cell-shape plots, designed to facilitate efficient analysis of morphological and developmental characteristics; and (3) an integrated, explainable machine learning classifier offering transparent, clinically-informed embryo viability scoring to predict live birth outcomes. Quantitative evaluation of our classifier and qualitative case studies conducted with practitioners demonstrate that EmbryoProfiler enables clinicians to make better-informed embryo selection decisions, potentially leading to improved clinical outcomes in IVF treatments.

2611.03410v1.title: OpenZilo: An Open Smart-Ring Platform for Human-Centric Sensing and Interaction with Robots
2611.03410v1.authors: Qianggang Ding, Xingyao Wang, Rui Feng, Chi Qin, Weijian Lin, Lizhi Ding, Jiankai Tang, Yuntao Wang, Xiangke Liu, Bang Liu
2611.03410v1.ori_summary: Wearable robot interfaces must connect user input to timely physical action. We present the proposed platform, an open smart-ring platform for studying this connection across task stages. The ring integrates a microphone, an inertial measurement unit, photoplethysmography, and skin-temperature sensing. Its software architecture separates acquisition, event interpretation, interaction policy, and robot execution. We characterize seven operating modes and evaluate speech and gesture control with 10 participants. Across five commands and 250 trials per modality, speech and gestures achieved task success rates of 90.4% and 88.8%, respectively. Recognition accuracy exceeded task success for both modalities. Gaussian hidden Markov models achieved higher accuracy than a support vector machine across three vocabulary sizes, with longer scoring times. Following a shared spoken task start, gesture-based adjustments had shorter median response times than speech. Whole-task success was 70.0% with gestures and 64.0% with speech. We further examine physiological-event-triggered robot interaction using simulated event notifications. Mean notification-receipt-to-arrival times were 11.71 s for the robot and 9.20 s for an on-site person. These descriptive findings support evaluating wearable robot interfaces through both recognition and physical outcomes, with timing measures appropriate to each task stage.

2611.03052v1.title: Selfrionette: A Fingertip Force-Input Controller for Continuous Full-Body Avatar Manipulation and Diverse Haptic Interactions
2611.03052v1.ori_summary: We propose Selfrionette, a controller that uses fingertip force input to drive avatar movements in virtual reality (VR). This system enables users to interact with virtual objects and walk in VR using only fingertip force, overcoming physical and spatial constraints. Additionally, by fixing users' fingers, it provides users with counterforces equivalent to the applied force, allowing for diverse and wide dynamic range haptic feedback by adjusting the relationship between force input and virtual movement. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, this paper focuses on hand interaction as a first step. In User Study 1, we measured usability and embodiment during reaching tasks under Selfrionette, body tracking, and finger tracking conditions. In User Study 2, we investigated whether users could perceive haptic properties such as weight, friction, and compliance under the same conditions as User Study 1. Selfrionette was found to be comparable to body tracking in realism of haptic interaction, enabling embodied avatar experiences even in limited spatial conditions.

2611.03023v1.title: VizDAGuide: Misleading Chart Question Answering in Compact Vision Language Models via DAG-Structured Supervision
2611.03023v1.authors: Haiyang Zhang, Sicheng Song, Zixin Chen, Jie Gu, Huiya Ou, Chenhui Li, Changbo Wang
2611.03023v1.ori_summary: Misleading charts can lead vision-language models to conclusions that conflict with underlying data. Existing work focuses on inference-time strategies, while training-time supervision remains less explored. We present VizDAGuide, a DAG-structured supervision method for misleading-chart question answering. The method represents intermediate reasoning states and their dependencies as a directed acyclic graph, assigns supervision weights according to their roles, and serializes the graph into a unified training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference. Experiments on two benchmarks across Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models show improvements over a content- and weight-matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline on both answer formats. Process-level evaluation shows gains in grounding and operation execution, while ablations indicate that dependency structure and weighted supervision are most effective when combined. These results support DAG-structured weighted supervision for misleading-chart question answering.

2611.03021v1.title: MetamorphX: An Ungrounded 3-DoF Moment Display that Changes its Physical Properties through Rotational Impedance Control
2611.03021v1.authors: Takeru Hashimoto, Shigeo Yoshida, Takuji Narumi
2611.03021v1.ori_summary: Humans can estimate the properties of wielded objects (e.g., inertia and viscosity) using the force applied to the hand. We focused on this mechanism and aimed to represent the properties of wielded objects by dynamically changing the force applied to the hand. We propose MetamorphX, which uses control moment gyroscopes (CMGs) to generate ungrounded, 3-degrees of freedom moment feedback. The high-response moments obtained from CMGs allow the inertia and viscosity of motion to be set to the desired values via impedance control. A technical evaluation indicated that our device can generate a moment with a 60-ms delay. The inertia and viscosity of motion were varied by $0.01\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and $0.1\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, respectively. Additionally, we demonstrated that our device can dynamically change the inertia and viscosity of motion through virtual reality applications.

2611.03018v1.title: How Data Journalists Visualize Uncertainty: Editorial Constraints and Design Heuristics in Newsroom Practice
2611.03018v1.authors: Carmen Garro, Annemarie Wisbar, Benjamin Possin, Christoph Kinkeldey
2611.03018v1.ori_summary: Communicating uncertainty is increasingly recognized as important in data journalism, yet in practice it is often oversimplified, downplayed, or omitted. To understand how uncertainty is handled in newsroom visualization practice, we conducted a full-day workshop with 11 data journalists from major German-speaking newsrooms. The workshop combined presentations of newsroom examples, collaborative scenario classification, World Café discussions on authoring hurdles, and group reflections on audience needs and future directions. Our findings suggest that uncertainty communication is primarily a workflow- and context-dependent editorial decision, constrained by production overhead, anticipated audience misinterpretation, publication formats, and the need to preserve a clear takeaway. Rather than relying on advanced visualization techniques, practitioners favor pragmatic defaults, layered communication, and explanatory guidance tailored to audience and medium. The scenario-based framework we provided is valued less as a strict taxonomy for classifying finished visualizations than as a planning prompt for early design reasoning. Based on these insights, we contribute (i) practitioner-informed findings on the challenges and strategies of visualizing uncertainty in journalistic practice, (ii) a refined scenario-based framework to support communication about uncertainty, and (iii) practice-oriented heuristics for designing uncertainty visualizations in newsrooms. Our work contributes to bridging visualization research and newsroom practice by grounding uncertainty communication in the realities of journalistic production. Supplemental material is available at https://osf.io/8j4ep.

2611.02988v1.title: Can You Predict the Next Mind? Toward Multi-Turn Multi-Party Mental World Modeling
2611.02988v1.ori_summary: While multimodal foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in physical world modeling, generation, and embodied reasoning, their capacity for dynamic mental world modeling remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on static mental state perception or short-horizon decision-making, overlooking the dynamic mental trajectories inherent in multi-party, multi-turn interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce M$^3$WME-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate mental world modeling conditioned on the evolving actions of interactants. Specifically, models are tasked with forecasting a target subject's future mental states and behaviors over extended social interactions. In addition to the benchmark suite, we construct M$^3$WME-23K, a dedicated training dataset, and establish a competitive baseline named MindNext-7B. Extensive evaluations across four representative paradigms (general MLLMs, emotion-specialized MLLMs, agentic frameworks, and World Foundation Models) reveal that current systems consistently struggle to anticipate forward-looking mental states. Mechanistic analyses further reveal that existing architectures fundamentally lack forward mental state transition dynamics. Our findings highlight a pivotal challenge in advancing agents from physical to mental world modeling, charting new directions for socially adaptive AI.

2611.02983v1.title: Supporting Habit Formation in Pre-Meal Photo Capture: A Longitudinal Study of Behavior Change Techniques
2611.02983v1.authors: Jun Fang, Yueying Suo, Yuntao Wang, Susu Wang, Xiaoyu Yang, Qiqi Liu, Chuangyu Ding, Yuanchun Shi
2611.02983v1.ori_summary: Pre-meal photo capture is lightweight only with a smartphone, yet habit formation requires repeatedly initiating and completing the action within the narrow window before the first bite. We examine how supports based on behavior change techniques can shape capture adherence, perceived habit, and support needs over time. Using a participant-informed selection process, we implemented three smartphone supports targeting Prompts/cues, Focus on past success, and Social support. We evaluated them in a five-week field study with 54 participants, spanning support, withdrawal, and reinstatement, followed by interviews and a three-week follow-up. Across 4,945 main meals, 63.9\% were confirmed pre-meal captures, and adherence was broadly maintained across phases. Perceived automaticity and spontaneous remembering improved mainly during initial support. As capture became more familiar, participants combined spontaneous remembering with deliberate strategies, reduced active feature use while continuing to value support availability, and carried the practice forward through accumulated records, familiar tools, and chosen relationships. These findings frame BCT support for pre-meal photo capture as a configurable arrangement. Systems should preserve a predictable capture pathway while adapting when, how, and through whom support remains available.

2611.02827v1.title: GraTED: Graph--Tensor EEG Decoding for Passenger Hazard Perception in Autonomous Vehicles
2611.02827v1.authors: Yuxuan Gu, Yingkai Yang, Qiyu Rao, Tania Stathaki, Danilo Mandic
2611.02827v1.ori_summary: Passenger electroencephalography (EEG) can reveal road risk through anticipatory responses before hazardous events and neural reactions around their onset. However, existing EEG decoding methods often map physiologically meaningful arrangement of electrodes onto artificial 2D grids and thus flatten the higher-order time-feature representations into matrices, obscuring meaningful structure in the data. To preserve and exploit the spatial and time-feature structure of EEG recordings, we propose the Graph-Tensor EEG Decoding Model (GraTED) for passenger risk prediction (RP) and danger identification (DI) in autonomous-vehicle scenarios. GraTED models the electrode arrangement as an undirected graph based on their scalp locations, using graph convolution to capture spatial dependencies and low-rank tensor classification to preserve the multidimensional time-feature structure, while controlling model complexity. Evaluated on the PassengerEEG dataset, comprising 11 participants and 45 hours of recordings, GraTED achieves the highest balanced accuracy, compared to the state-of-the-art, across all three evaluation settings, while requiring the fewest learnable parameters among seven baseline methods.

2611.02801v1.title: Analysing the Narrative Paradox through Formal Models and Properties in Interactive Narrative
2611.02801v1.authors: Jules Clerc, Mohamed Sallak, Domitile Lourdeaux, Marc Ravaine
2611.02801v1.ori_summary: Interactive narratives aim to let players influence the unfolding of a story while preserving a coherent and satisfying narrative progression. This creates a central tension, commonly described as the narrative paradox, between player autonomy and narrative control. Experience Managers (EMs) manage the story by determining how the narrative progresses in response to player behaviour. Although this paradox is widely discussed, it is rarely modelled in a way that supports systematic analysis, simulation, and comparison across management strategies. This paper proposes a formal framework for modelling and analysing the narrative paradox as a trade-off between interdependent properties shaped by EM decisions. We represent interactive narrative behaviour through an extended state-transition system in which world states are connected by player actions and system events. From this model, we formalize key properties involved in the paradox such as the player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness, and define quantitative indicators derived from simulated plans. These indicators make it possible to compare EM strategies according to their ability to balance freedom, control, and narrative satisfaction. A case study compares different EM policies, showing how simulations can reveal correlations and conflicts between properties and identify compromise zones in the design space. This work contributes a reusable modelling and analysis framework for studying the narrative paradox and evaluating heterogeneous interactive narratives on shared formal grounds, with a focus on supporting the comparison and testing of EM strategies.

2611.02790v1.title: MultiMental-IAS: A Multimodal Driver Mental State Analysis Dataset for Context-Aware Non-IID Evaluation
2611.02790v1.authors: Baran Can Gül, Nagendra Pal Singh, Anjana Arvind Naik
2611.02790v1.ori_summary: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.

2611.02623v1.title: Ask More, Hear Less: How a Review Prompt Changes What Online Ratings Show
2611.02623v1.authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
2611.02623v1.ori_summary: Platforms ask customers for online reviews to reduce self-selection, but theory conflicts on whether review solicitation makes online ratings more or less informative. Selection theory implies that asking helps, voice theory that it dilutes the news, and research on rating inflation that compression destroys information. We reconcile these views with signal detection theory, which separates what a rating knows (its sensitivity) from what it shows (its criterion). We test the framework on Steam, a leading PC video game store, whose client began in October 2019 to prompt players for a review after about three hours of play. Using a difference-in-discontinuities design at that inferred threshold in 21.6 million Steam reviews of 315 games, we find that review counts just above the threshold become 4.25 times those just below, and the jump in the positive share grows by 6.6 percentage points. Agreement with critics changes little near launch and erodes later. The rating's movement changes far more: pass-through from reviews written in the first two hours falls from 0.73 to 0.18 just above the threshold, against 0.81 to 0.64 just below, and a fixed rating tier responds to 12% of downturns in those reviews above the threshold, down from 42%, against 41% and 47% below it. What the stream knows changes less. At equal review counts its sensitivity falls more above the threshold, because added reviews respond about half as much and scores near the ceiling are noisier per review, but at natural counts added volume offsets this loss, leaving a change of -0.03 relative to the stream below (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06). Failures that developers acknowledge, which run through complaints, still move the score after launch. Review prompts therefore mainly change how a rating must be read, and platforms that solicit reviews should recalibrate their rating labels.

2611.02599v1.title: Camera-Free Object Discovery and Interaction with GazeTags
2611.02599v1.ori_summary: We present GazeTags, a camera- and computer-vision-free approach for worn head-gaze object awareness. Our small electronic tags cost roughly \$2 each and can operate for more than a year on a coin cell battery. They work in concert with a user-worn device (smartglasses, hearables, etc.) that periodically emits a focused infrared signal aligned with the user's head direction. Only GazeTags within that narrow head-oriented beam wake and respond, providing their identity and optional payloads such as object state or live sensor readings. By avoiding cameras and computer vision pipelines, our approach is very energy efficient, able to operate continuously even in battery-constrained wearables, and sidesteps non-trivial privacy issues. We describe our hardware design, characterize our system performance and operating tradeoffs, and demonstrate how GazeTags can enable practical gaze-aware environments.

2611.02525v1.title: Touching Projected Agents through the DAT Screen -System Design and Questions of Interaction Boundaries-
2611.02525v1.ori_summary: Touching a virtual agent involves more than detecting a finger on a display: the contact surface can deform and resist the user's push, and the agent can respond to that action. We describe the Desktop Amid Touch (DAT) screen, which combines spatial projection onto a semi-transparent, deformable mesh with touch sensing and motorized control of resistance to indentation. An initial prototype detected a single touch and estimated its position and depth from tension changes around a flexible projection screen. A subsequent prototype added motorized tension control to vary the screen's resistance to indentation. We describe the tension-controlled DAT implementation and its demonstrations, distinguishing what has been observed from what remains an open design question. These capabilities raise a design question: should touchable virtual agents respond as though they had preferences or boundaries, and under what conditions should such behavior be implemented on systems like DAT. The present paper describes a system and frames this question; it does not establish how users interpret an agent's refusal or consent.

2611.02517v1.title: A Study on the Effects of Finger Movements on a Humanoid Hugging Robot
2611.02517v1.ori_summary: This study aimed to examine the impact of finger movements in hugging robots on users by experimentally investigating how the presence and patterns of such movements affect users psychologically. The results suggest that the presence and patterns of finger movements influence the sensations users seek from the robot; specifically, repetitive movements and asynchronous movements across multiple fingers tended to enhance these sensations. Additionally, simultaneous movement of all fingers and gentle hugging tended to evoke a greater sense of care. Conversely, no differences were observed regarding resistance to physical contact initiated by the robot.

2611.02490v1.title: How Contextual Information in Physical Environments Shapes Decisions with AI
2611.02490v1.authors: Omar Elgohary, Amanda Elvarsdottir, Vannessa Lee, Zhu-Tian Chen
2611.02490v1.ori_summary: We studied whether contextual information helps people make better decisions with fallible AI in a partially visible environment. In an AR study (N = 32), participants judged whether a rendered key was present on a physical desk, with or without AI advice. We varied target prevalence and scene visibility. Focal analyses excluded visible targets and AI suggestions that could be directly checked. Within this subset, the combined context of a stronger prior toward absence (lower prevalence) and a target-free half increased AI-assisted accuracy by 9.5 percentage points. An exploratory analysis accounted for most of this increase through changes in the cases and AI suggestions being evaluated; changed participant responses did not significantly improve accuracy beyond maintaining baseline response patterns. The stronger prior reduced agreement with Present suggestions, while the target-free half lengthened decision time. We did not detect more selective agreement with correct versus incorrect advice. These findings motivate evaluating situated assistance on matched cases and designing ways to obtain evidence that can resolve claims about hidden states.

2611.02467v1.title: A dynamic backrest may help accommodate trunk movement, and multi-device work elicits more of it: An exploratory comparison of high-end office chairs under single- and multi-device tasks
2611.02467v1.authors: Yejin Kang, Dusan Baek, Dongwoo Park, Kitae Hwang, Woojin Park
2611.02467v1.ori_summary: Dynamic-sitting office chairs are usually compared with static sitting rather than with each other, and the contribution of backrest deformability (lateral backrest movement) is unknown. Office work also increasingly spans multiple devices. Twenty healthy adults (10 men, 10 women) completed a 15-minute single-device and a 15-minute multi-device proofreading task on each of three chairs: two commercial dynamic-sitting chairs (T90, Aeron) and a T90 whose backrest lateral movement was mechanically fixed (T90-fixed). We recorded subjective ratings, head and trunk posture (inertial measurement units), upper trapezius and lateral gastrocnemius activity (electromyography), and task performance. Chair effects were largely null: T90 and Aeron did not differ in ratings or performance, posture and muscle activity showed only isolated, direction-inconsistent differences, and preferences were polarized. The standard T90 showed greater trunk movement (mean absolute angular velocity in yaw) than T90-fixed during the multi-device task (p = 0.042), which may indicate that its movable backrest helps accommodate trunk movement under demanding work; no other whole-sample posture, muscle, rating or performance measure differed between these two configurations, and replication is needed. Task effects were large and consistent: the multi-device task elicited greater and faster head, trunk and shoulder movement and higher upper trapezius activity than the single-device task, with lower reading throughput. Multi-device work thus imposes substantially greater movement demands than single-device work, which supports designing chairs that accommodate movement in modern work environments.

2611.02452v1.title: Adjustment control usability and dynamic accommodation in office chairs: A comparative study of two contemporary designs
2611.02452v1.authors: Yejin Kang, Dusan Baek, Dongwoo Park, Kitae Hwang, Woojin Park
2611.02452v1.ori_summary: Adjustability is a core determinant of ergonomic fit in office chairs, but its benefits depend on users being able to operate the controls and, on the chair, continuing to support the body as posture changes during work. We compared two high-end office chairs, the T90 (Sidiz; Chair A) and the Aeron (Herman Miller; Chair B), in two experiments to explore which design features may explain differences between them. In Experiment 1, 20 participants adjusted ten controls common to both chairs and rated perceived adjustment difficulty on four items. Chair A had significantly lower overall difficulty (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.008), with control-level advantages for headrest angle, armrest height, armrest rotation angle and lumbar support position; Chair B was easier for seat height, possibly because its side-mounted lever is more visible than Chair A's underside button. The headrest comparisons involved a third-party headrest fitted to Chair B, and control- and item-level tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons. In Experiment 2, the same participants completed a 15-minute multi-device task requiring repeated posture changes, reach and reorientation, then rated body-part discomfort, general comfort and satisfaction with five components. Discomfort and comfort did not differ; Chair A had higher satisfaction for the seat-pan and lumbar support (exploratory, uncorrected). Interviews suggested links to mechanism properties: Chair B's rear lumbar dial was often described as producing little perceptible change, and for controls without significant differences each chair appeared to leave a different aspect of the same need unmet. These findings suggest mechanical and interface properties that designers of adjustable office chairs may consider for dynamic, multi-device work.

2611.02447v1.title: DruMR: A Feedback Driven Mixed Reality Air Drumming System
2611.02447v1.authors: Omar Elgohary, Viktor Radev, James Herbert, Akul Manoj
2611.02447v1.ori_summary: This paper introduces DruMR, a mixed reality (MR) drumming system designed to make learning drums more accessible, responsive, and feedback-driven. By combining Aerodrums hardware with the Meta Quest 3 headset, DruMR allows users to drum in a virtual environment without a physical drum set. Unlike existing VR drumming applications, DruMR emphasizes instructional value through quantitative feedback and future integration of AI-generated insights, refined quantitative and qualitative visualizations, reactive environment modes and more. Overall, this paper reviews the current state of the DruMR system, related works that influenced the systems development, planned user study comparing physical and virtual training, and future work to be added to the system.

2611.02410v1.title: Spatial Organization Is Accessibility Structure: Hierarchical Screen Reading of Mobile UIs
2611.02410v1.authors: Yongxiang Hu, Xuan Wang, Qingyang Qiu, Yingjie Liu, Chun Kang, Ruiying Zeng, Xin Wang, Yangfan Zhou
2611.02410v1.ori_summary: Screen readers for blind and low-vision (BLV) users flatten mobile UIs into a linear sequence. Modern mobile UIs, however, contain dozens of elements grouped by spatial layout. Such linear access is ill-suited for BLV users, who must infer each element's meaning and which elements form a functional unit. Drawing on a quantitative TalkBack audit and formative interviews, we present Spatial Screen Reader (SeeR), which builds a function-aware hierarchy from accessibility metadata and provides unit summaries with hierarchical navigation. Compared with TalkBack, SeeR reduces non-informative focus stops by 82.1% and navigation steps by 52.7%. With ten BLV participants, summaries helped them connect controls to their functions and skip nonessential elements, especially on unfamiliar pages, though extra navigation levels added effort when the target was already known. These findings recast spatial organization as accessibility information: apps and platforms should expose it, rather than leaving screen readers to infer it post hoc.

2611.02393v1.title: IMUdrape: Generating Garment-Mounted Virtual IMU Data from Text through Physics-Based Cloth Simulation
2611.02393v1.ori_summary: Inertial sensors are moving into clothing, from sensorized sportswear to garments instrumented with hundreds of IMUs. Sewn into clothing, a sensor no longer moves rigidly with the body: loose fabric slides, twists and swings, so a garment-mounted sensor records the motion of the fabric as well as that of the body, and this extra motion differs from one garment to the next. Models for such sensors need training data recorded with the deployed garment, yet labeled data are scarce. Virtual IMU data generated from videos or text have eased this scarcity for body-attached sensors, but existing generators attach their virtual sensors rigidly to the body. We present IMUdrape, which generates garment-mounted virtual IMU data from text through physics-based cloth simulation. IMUdrape synthesizes motion from activity descriptions, reconstructs the target garment as a sewing pattern from photographs, places virtual IMUs at the deployment's real sensor positions, and simulates the garment with an intersection-free contact solver, so that every simulation yields paired garment and body signals. On four real datasets with clothing-mounted sensors, IMUdrape improves on existing virtual-data approaches for both activity recognition and full-body pose estimation. With one real subject, its data improve recognition macro-F1 by 7% to 46% over real data alone and by 2% to 11% over body-mounted virtual data from the same motion. When the garment is simulated on recorded motion, the pose error without any real training data falls by 30% to 33% relative to generated motion, and garment data remain 12% more accurate than body data. IMUdrape thus reduces the amount of real data that garment-mounted sensing requires.
